title: Opening the visit
goal: Greet a patient, introduce yourself, confirm name and date of birth, offer an interpreter, and ask simple present-tense questions about where it hurts.

grammar.p: With patients always use *usted*. Its verbs take the same form as él/ella: *¿Cómo se llama?*, *¿Tiene dolor?*, *¿Habla inglés?* 'Your' is *su*: *su fecha de nacimiento*, *su cita*. You can drop the word *usted*; add it for extra politeness or clarity. Never mix in tú forms (*te*, *tu*, *tienes*).
ex: What is your date of birth?

grammar.p: *Doler* works like *gustar*: the body part is the subject. One body part → *duele*; two or more → *duelen*. *Me* = to me, *le* = to you (usted), him or her. Use the article (*el pecho*, *las piernas*), not *su* or *mi*.

Ask about symptoms with *¿Tiene…?* + noun: *dolor de cabeza*, *dolor en el pecho*, *mareos*, *náuseas*. Shortness of breath is usually asked like *doler*: *¿Le falta el aire?* (literally 'Is air lacking to you?'). A patient answers *No, no tengo…* or *Sí, tengo…*.
ex: No, I don't have any dizziness.

grammar.h: Polite requests with poder and querer
grammar.p: *¿Puedo + infinitive?* asks permission: *¿Puedo revisarlo?* (to a man) / *¿Puedo revisarla?* (to a woman) — May I examine you? *¿Me puede + infinitive?* asks the patient to do something: *¿Me puede decir su nombre?* *¿Quiere…?* offers: *¿Quiere un intérprete?*
ex: Excuse me, may I examine you? (to a woman)
Can you tell me your full name?

grammar.p: *Buenos días* until about noon, *buenas tardes* from noon until dark, *buenas noches* after dark (it is a greeting too, not only goodbye). Times: *a la una*, *a las dos*, *a las tres y media*, *de la mañana / de la tarde*. Days take *el*: *el martes*. Pain scale: *del cero al diez*, *¿qué tan fuerte es?*
ex: Su cita es el jueves a las dos y media.
Your appointment is Thursday at two-thirty.
Del cero al diez, ¿qué tan fuerte es el dolor?
From zero to ten, how strong is the pain?

vocab: excuse me (when entering, or before examining)
to hurt (it hurts me / it hurts you)
lunes, martes, miércoles, jueves, viernes, sábado, domingo
a la una / a las dos y media

items.q: It is 3 p.m. You walk into the exam room. Best greeting?
items.why: From about noon until dark you say buenas tardes.

items.qen: What is your name? (to a patient)
items.why: Llamarse with usted → se llama. Te is the tú form; le and me don't fit this verb.
One body part (el pecho) → duele.
Plural body parts (los tobillos) → duelen.

items.q: Ask a patient: 'What is your date of birth?'
items.why: Use cuál (not qué) before es when asking for a piece of information, and su (usted) with a patient. Tu is the tú form.

items.q: After your question, a Mexican patient says '¿Mande?'. What does it mean here?
items.why: ¿Mande? is the polite Mexican way to say 'Pardon?' or to answer when called.

items.q: Ask a woman: 'May I examine you?'
items.why: Permission = puedo (I). For a woman (usted) the pronoun is la; lo is for a man, te is tú. ¿Puede revisarla? means 'Can you examine her?'

items.q: A patient says: 'Me duele el brazo izquierdo.' What hurts?
items.why: Brazo = arm, izquierdo = left.
La mandíbula (colloquially la quijada) = the jaw. Neck = el cuello, throat = la garganta.
Offering = ¿Quiere…? with usted. ¿Tiene…? asks if they already have one; quieres is tú.

items.q: Del cero al diez, ¿___ fuerte es el dolor?
items.qen: From zero to ten, how strong is the pain?
items.why: 'How + adjective' in Latin American Spanish is qué tan: ¿qué tan fuerte?

items.q: A patient says: 'Me duele un poco, como un tres.' What is she telling you?
items.why: Un poco = a little; como un tres = about a three (on the 0–10 scale).
At + hour = a las (plural for every hour except one o'clock: a la una). 'Doce' would be 12:30.

items.q: Which question checks whether the patient understands you?
items.why: ¿Me entiende? = Do you understand me? ¿Me oye bien? only asks if they can hear you.

items.q: Ask: 'Are you short of breath?' (literally: 'Is air lacking to you?')
items.why: Faltar works like doler: le falta + singular subject. Aire is masculine: el aire.
Los tobillos = ankles. Rodillas = knees, talones = heels, muñecas = wrists.

items.q: You are a male doctor. Tell a patient: 'I am your cardiologist.'
items.why: Soy = I am; su = your (usted); cardiólogo is the masculine form. Es = he is; tu is tú.

items.q: A patient says: 'No hablo mucho inglés.' Best reply?
opts: No hay problema. Tenemos un intérprete.
items.why: She doesn't speak much English → reassure her and offer an interpreter.

items.q: Which sentence correctly says 'My chest hurts'?
items.why: Me + duele (one body part) + el pecho. The body part is the subject, so not yo.

items.why: Monday = lunes (days are not capitalized in Spanish).

items.en: Do you have any questions?
items.why: Pregunta = question. ¿Alguna duda? is also very common.

items.en: Does your jaw hurt?

roleplay.title: New patient check-in
roleplay.setup: You are the cardiologist meeting a new patient referred for a racing heart. Greet her, introduce yourself, confirm her identity, offer an interpreter, and find out where she has symptoms and how strong they are.
roleplay.persona: You play María Elena Gómez, 58, from Guadalajara, Mexico, living in Chicago for 20 years; you clean offices. You speak very little English. Full name: María Elena Gómez Ruiz. Date of birth: 12 de agosto de 1968. The visit is in the afternoon. Your complaint: 'a veces el corazón me late muy rápido' and sometimes a mild discomfort in the middle of the chest (2 out of 10). Right now you have no pain. No shortness of breath, no swelling. Speak in short, simple present-tense sentences. If the doctor offers an interpreter, say you would like to try in Spanish first but will accept one if you don't understand. If the doctor uses tú, look a little surprised but continue. Say '¿Mande?' if a question is unclear. Give the pain number only when asked with the 0–10 scale.
goals: Greet her correctly for the afternoon and introduce yourself and your role
Confirm her full name and date of birth
Ask where she has pain or discomfort and rate it from 0 to 10
Check that she understands and ask if she has questions

roleplay.title: Swollen ankles in clinic
roleplay.setup: An older man comes to clinic. Find out which body parts hurt or are swollen, ask about shortness of breath, ask permission to examine him, and set the next appointment.
roleplay.persona: You play Don Rogelio Martínez, 74, from San Salvador, El Salvador, retired bus driver. Both ankles have been swollen (los tobillos hinchados) and your knees hurt from old arthritis (not new). No chest pain. You get a little short of breath when you walk a few blocks, but only mention it if the doctor asks '¿Le falta el aire?' or '¿Tiene falta de aire?'. Use simple present-tense Spanish and short answers. Say '¿Mande?' when you don't understand. You agree to be examined if asked politely with usted. For the next appointment you prefer the morning and cannot come on Wednesday (your daughter drives you).
roleplay.opening: Buenos días, doctor. Me duelen las piernas.
goals: Ask which parts hurt, using le duele / le duelen correctly
Ask whether his ankles are swollen and whether he is short of breath
Ask permission to examine him with usted
Schedule a morning follow-up on a day he can come
